title: Problem set 15: Electrochemical instrumentation
summary: Practice with the potentiostat and its building blocks: iR drop, current measurement, time constants, iR compensation and noise reduction.

intro.text: A potentiostat sets the working-electrode potential relative to a reference while the counter electrode passes the current. Key relations are the iR drop V = iR, the current-to-voltage conversion V = i Rf, and the response time tau = RC.
Positive feedback compensates most of the iR drop but cannot reach 100 percent without instability.

sections.title: Hint sheet: instrumentation relations
sections.summary: Practice with the potentiostat and its building blocks: iR drop, current measurement, time constants, iR compensation and noise reduction.
keyPoints: Reference in a high-impedance sense circuit

blocks.text: A potentiostat sets the working-electrode potential relative to a reference while the counter electrode passes the current. Key relations are the iR drop V = iR, the current-to-voltage conversion V = i Rf, and the response time tau = RC.
Positive feedback compensates most of the iR drop but cannot reach 100 percent without instability.

questions.question: A current of 1.0 mA flows through an uncompensated resistance of 100 ohm. Calculate the iR drop in volts.
questions.explanation: iR = 1.0e-3 x 100 = 0.1 V. This error adds directly to the measured working-electrode potential.

questions.question: A current-to-voltage converter has a feedback resistor of 1.0 Mohm. What output voltage in volts corresponds to an input current of 1.0 uA? (V = i Rf.)
A potentiostat has an effective series resistance of 1.0 Mohm and the cell capacitance is 10 pF. Calculate the response time constant in microseconds (tau = RC).
If the total iR drop is 0.1 V, what residual iR error in volts remains after 90 percent positive-feedback compensation?
questions.explanation: Residual = 10 percent of 0.1 V = 0.010 V. Positive feedback can never be pushed to 100 percent without instability.

questions.question: In a three-electrode cell the potentiostat controls the potential of the:
options: Working electrode relative to the reference electrode
Counter electrode relative to itself
Reference electrode relative to the counter electrode
Solution relative to the counter electrode
questions.explanation: The working electrode potential is measured against the reference and held at the set value; the counter electrode passes whatever current is needed.

questions.question: In a three-electrode cell the faradaic current flows between the working and counter electrodes, not through the reference electrode.
questions.explanation: The reference electrode is kept in a high-impedance sense circuit so almost no current flows through it, preserving its stable potential.

questions.question: Positive feedback iR compensation works by:
options: Increasing the applied voltage to offset the measured iR drop
Grounding the reference electrode
Removing the supporting electrolyte
Reducing the cell capacitance to zero
questions.explanation: The instrument senses the cell current, multiplies it by a fraction of the measured resistance and adds that voltage back, cancelling most of the iR drop.

questions.question: Overcompensating the iR drop with positive feedback can make the potentiostat unstable and oscillate.
questions.explanation: Pushing compensation beyond 100 percent creates positive feedback that the control loop cannot handle, so the system oscillates.

questions.question: Which are good practices in electrochemical instrumentation? Select all that apply.
options: Use a Faraday cage and shielding to reduce noise
Keep the reference tip close to the working electrode
Use a high-input-impedance reference sense circuit
Connect the reference electrode directly to carry the cell current
questions.explanation: Shielding reduces noise, a close reference tip reduces iR, and a high-impedance sense circuit keeps current off the reference. Carrying the cell current through the reference would destroy its stable potential.

questions.question: An instrument can resolve currents to 1.0 pA. If the full-scale current is 1.0 mA, what is the dynamic range as a factor (full scale / resolution)?
questions.explanation: Dynamic range = 1.0e-3/1.0e-12 = 1.0e9, i.e. nine orders of magnitude.

questions.question: A current-to-voltage converter has a feedback resistor of 1.0 Gohm. What output voltage in volts corresponds to an input current of 10 nA? (V = i Rf.)
A current of 10 uA flows through an uncompensated resistance of 1.0 kohm. Calculate the iR drop in volts.
A potentiostat maintains the working-electrode potential by:
options: Feeding back a current through the counter electrode so the reference senses the set potential
Grounding the counter electrode
Disconnecting the reference
Heating the cell
questions.explanation: The control amplifier drives the counter electrode until the working electrode, sensed against the reference, sits at the set potential.

questions.question: A reference electrode is deliberately kept out of the current-carrying path to preserve its stable potential.
questions.explanation: Because the reference is sensed with a high-impedance input, negligible current flows through it, so its potential does not drift during the experiment.

questions.question: Which reduce noise in a sensitive electrochemical measurement? Select all that apply.
options: A Faraday cage around the cell
Short, shielded leads
A clean, stable reference electrode
Loosely twisted, unshielded wires across a power supply
questions.explanation: Shielding, short leads and a stable reference all reduce noise. Unshielded wiring near a power supply adds noise rather than removing it.
